BOPEN.heard: Building virtual environments exam prep, key terms, the walkthrough film, 32 terms for planning, routing, recording and finishing a film that moves a camera through a game you built, and for proving that what the film says is true.

BIDEA.heard: Hollow, this is Liam in for bear. Newcomers often think a walkthrough film is there to make a game look good, it is not. It shows what the game really does from real captures and says plainly what it leaves out. This film goes through the terms for planning, routing, recording, and checking such a film, each one shown.

BDEFS.heard: Eight labels sit in the corners of the pictures that follow. In the book text, the course text uses and explains the term. In the glossary, the term is on the course term list, but the text does not explain it. Video only, the term comes from the course's film skills and assignment briefs. Outside source, the term comes from a source outside the course text, computed. The numbers are worked out on screen from stated inputs. Simulation, a model run step by step from stated rules, not a measurement of a real game. Illustrative data, numbers chosen to show the idea, not measured, conceptual, a drawing of the idea with no data behind it.

B0101.heard: This table is the map 32 terms in four groups for a film that moves a camera through a game. The first group planet holds walkthrough film, central idea, beat, beat sheet, storyboards, script, voiceover and pacing, what the film says in what order for how long.

B0102.heard: The second group routed holds shot, route, waypoint, establishing shot, camera move and route check. These terms say where the camera goes and how you check that its path is allowed before a single frame is made.

B0103.heard: The third group record it holds real-time capture, render, fixed frame rate, deterministic capture, frame rate, frame count, resolution and aspect ratio. These terms say how the frames of the film are made.

B0104.heard: The fourth group, Finish and Check, holds cut and transition, be roll, title card, safe margins, captions, decibel loudness, what it is not, call to action and claim versus evidence. These terms say how the film is put together and how it is proved honest.

B0201.heard: A drawing of a level with a red camera frame sweeping across it. A walk-through film is a narrated camera tour of a game or an asset. It shows what the thing really does from real captures and says what it leaves out. Its parts are camera moves voice over and a plain statement of what it is not. For example, a student films one level of their platformer up to the flag, while the narration says there is no save system yet.

B0202.heard: Central idea is the one sentence every shot in the film must serve. A shot that does not serve it is cut, even a good looking one. In this made up example the idea is that level one teaches the jump. Four of six candidate shots serve it and the menu music reel and the credits scroll are cut. For example, if a student's film is about how an enemy patrols, a pretty shot of the title menu does not belong in it.

B0203.heard: A beat is one unit of the film, one picture, one idea, and the word spoken over it. In this made-up beat, the picture is the jump over the first gap. The idea is that a longer press jumps farther, and its 13 words take 5.4 seconds at 2.4 words a second. For example, one beat might show the player touching a coin, while a single line says that each coin adds to the score.

B0204.heard: A beat sheet is the whole film as a table, each beats picture, words, and length in order. It is also the shot list, one row per shot. Here's six made up beats, run six plus twelve plus eighteen plus twenty plus sixteen plus ten, eighty two seconds, a summon, not a target. A storyboard has only pictures, and a beat sheet adds words and seconds. For example, a student lists each beat of their platformer film with its line in its seconds. Before capturing anything.

B0301.heard: Four rough frames, a gap, a jump, a spike, and a flag. A storyboard is a set of rough drawings of the key frames in order made before anything is captured. It fixes what each picture will show with no words and no seconds yet. For example, before recording a film of their dungeon game, a student sketches four boxes on paper, the door, the first enemy, the key, and the exit, one per beat.

B0302.heard: Under each frame now sits a line of narration. The script is those words written out and checked before anyone records them. Written under each frame they can be counted and cut. Here the four lines have nine, fourteen, fifteen and seventeen words. The script is the words on paper and the voiceover is the same word spoken. For example, a student filming a racing game writes the line for the first corner, counts its words and trims it before recording.

B0303.heard: Voice over is narration heard over the pictures, while the speaker is never shown in the shot. Speaking takes time. At 2.4 words a second, nine words take 3.8 seconds and 17 takes 7.1. The four lines add up to 22.9 seconds of speech. For example, in a film of a puzzle game, the narrator explains how a switch opens a door while the viewer sees only the game, never the narrator.

B0304.heard: Pacing is how long each beat lasts, set by the stretch of route the camera must cover and the time its words need. Speech must fit its beat, beats 1 and 3 fit. Beat 2 has 5.8 seconds of speech and a 5 second beat, so two words go and beat 4 loses one word. You cut words, not footage. For example, the line spoken while the camera crosses a bridge and a student's level must end before the camera leaves the bridge.

B0401.heard: A top view of a level 38 by 22 meters with walls and five small landmarks. A shot is one continuous camera take with a job revealing something no earlier shot did. This one covers the first leg nine meters at one meter a second so nine seconds. The route is the whole path and a shot is one take along part of it. For example, one shot follows a student's player character from the start to the first pit without a cut.

B0402.heard: Route is the planned path the camera travels through the scene, measured before any frame is rendered. Here the camera runs the whole red line 43 meters. Divide that length by the speed 1 meter a second and you get the running time 43 seconds. For example, before recording a film of a cave level, a student plans the camera's path from the entrance past the bats to the treasure room and measures how long it is.

B0403.heard: A waypoint is a point along the route where the camera passes, turns, or stops. Five numbered waypoints split this route into four legs, nine, ten, fourteen, and ten meters, forty-three, and all. Each leg can be its own shot, and the waypoints turn a wish for the camera into numbers. For example, a student puts one waypoint at the level's start, one where the camera turns toward a moving platform, and one at the goal flag where it stops.

B0404.heard: An establishing shot is a wide opening shot that shows where everything is before any near view. The red frame takes in all five landmarks at once. The black box, the first near view, holds only one of the five. For example, a walkthrough of a small arena game might open on the whole arena from above, so the viewer knows where the spawn points and the exit are before the camera moves in on the player.

B0501.heard: Four small top views a pan, a dolly in, a truck in an orbit. A camera moves with the camera itself does, such as turning on the spot, moving toward the subject, sliding sideways or circling it. Each one can be measured. This pan turns 40 degrees in 4 seconds, 10 degrees a second, under a limit of 30. For example, in a film of their level, a slow orbit around a statue the student modeled in Blender shows it from every side.

B0502.heard: A route check is a script that steps through every frame of the route, measuring speed, turn rate, roll and height. The camera moves as what the camera does and the route check says whether it is allowed. Over 30 meters and 24 seconds, linear keys hold 1.25 meters a second, while an ease from rest peaks at 1.96 over the 1.5 limit. For example, a student checks the path through their forest level before recording.

B0503.heard: The route checks result as a table with made-up measured values. Linear speed, turn rate, roll, and eye height pass. Ease speed 1.96 meters a second fails. One fail sends you back to fix the route, not the report, and the limits are starting points, not standards. For example, if the camera dips below eye height on a staircase in a student's level, they raise the path and run the route check again.

B0601.heard: Milliseconds per frame for 36 frames of a simulated run. Real-time capture means recording the game while it runs, at whatever pace the machine manages so frame times vary. The dashed line is the 60 frames per second budget, 16.7 milliseconds. Nine of 36 frames took over one and a half times that so the take is hard to repeat. For example, a student screen records their platformer while playing it. And a busy explosion makes some frames late.

B0602.heard: Render means computing each frame offline as slowly as needed, then joining the frames into a film. In this simulated case a 10 second film at 30 frames per second is 300 frames, and at 4 seconds a frame it takes 20 minutes. Slow is fine, but a render proves nothing about how fast the game runs. For example, a student lets Blender render a turntable of their model overnight, frame by frame for a smooth clip of it.

B0603.heard: Fixed frame rate means every frame stands for exactly the same slice of game time, one divided by the frame rate, whatever the machine does. I fixed 30 frames per second, each frame is 33.3 milliseconds of game time, so 36 frames are 1.2 seconds on any machine. For example, a student launches their game from the command line with Godot's fixed frame rate option. So even a slow laptop moves the game forward by the same step, each frame.

B0604.heard: Deterministic capture gives the same frames every take from a fixed frame rate, the same inputs and the same route. In this simulation, game time reaches one second on frame 38 in one real time take and frame 48 in another. A fixed 60 frames per second it lands on frame 60 take after take. For example, a student records a jump with scripted inputs at a fixed rate, labels it as scripted, and a second take matches the first. Frame for frame.

B0701.heard: Rose of Tick marks one second each. Frame rate is how many frames are shown each second. The top row has 24 ticks, the middle 30, and the red row 60. Film often uses 24 or 30 in game 60. Resolution counts pixels in one frame, and frame rate counts frames in one second. For example, a student sets their walkthrough capture to 60 frames per second so their characters fast, dash, stay smooth.

B0702.heard: Frame count is frame rate times duration, the number of frames the film needs. For a 10 second film that is 240 frames at 24, 300 at 30, and 600 at 60. Every frame is stored or rendered, so 60 frames per second doubles the work of 30. For example, before rendering a boss fight clip from their game, a student works out its frame count to see how many frames the render must make.

B0703.heard: Resolution is the width and height of a frame in pixels. The nested boxes share one shape and hold about 0.92, 2.07, and 8.29 million pixels. Doubling width and height gives four times the pixels. Native capture means 3,840 by 2,160 from the start, not scaled up, for example. A student captures their game at that size, so the small numbers on the score display stay sharp.

B0704.heard: Aspect ratio is width divided by height. A landscape 16 by 9 frame is 1.78. A tall 9 by 16 frame is 0.56 and a square is exactly 1. Turned on its side, a frame keeps its pixels, but not its aspect. A landscape film in a vertical clip are two renders, not one crop. For example, for a phone-shaped clip, a student renders again in the tall shape instead of cutting the sides off the wide film.

B0801.heard: Two five second clips join two ways. A cut jumps straight to the next shot. A transition such as a dissolve overlaps the two shots for a moment. With a hard cut each clip stays whole, 10 seconds and all. A one second dissolve eats its overlap so the pair lasts nine seconds. For example, a student cuts straight from the player at the castle door to the player inside, but dissolves slowly from the day version of a level to the night version.

B0802.heard: B-roll is extra footage laid over the main capture. The main capture carries the claim, and the B-roll only decorates it. Here three seconds of B-roll sit over ten seconds of real capture. The narration runs unbroken, and the film is still ten seconds long. Constructed B-roll is labeled as constructed. For example, while the capture shows the player crossing a bridge, a student cuts in a short shot of the bridge model turning on its own. Labeled as a constructed view.

B0803.heard: A title card is a full-screen card carrying the film's name shown briefly at the start and at the end. Here it reads Walker Jumpman, a walkthrough. In this made-up film it takes 6 seconds of 82, about 7 percent the shortest beat of the film. For example, a student opens the film of their dungeon game with a dark card naming the game and shows the same card again for a moment at the very end.

B0901.heard: A frame 3,840 by 2,160 with a dashed box inside. Safe margins are that inner area, instead about 5% on each side where text and logos must sit. That is 192 pixels at each side and 108 at top and bottom. The red bar is text in the margin, which some screens crop. For example, a student places each level's name label inside the dashed line. Never along the top edge.

B0902.heard: Captions are the narration as text, burned into the picture, or kept in a separate subtitle file, each line with a start and an end time. This line walker stands at the first gap, runs from second one to second four. Thirty-one characters in three seconds is about ten characters a second. Captions are text you see in the voice-overs sound you hear. For example, a student's film of their stealth game shows a caption under each spoken line inside the safe area.

B0903.heard: Bars of amplitude beside their values in decibels. Decibel-written DB or DBFS is a logarithmic unit of loudness. Having the amplitude is about minus six decibels, and a tenth is minus 20. In digital audio, zero DBFS decibels relative to full scale is the largest level and everything sits below it. For example, when a student turns a coin sound in their game down to minus six decibels. Its wave becomes about half as tall.

B0904.heard: Loudness in Lough's Loudness Unit's relative to full scale is how loud the whole film is on average checked against a target window. One course film measured minus 24.55 inside a window of minus 28 to minus 18. Its true peak minus 2.96 sits under a ceiling of minus 1 about two decibels to spare. For example, a student measures their finished walkthrough finds its average below the window. And rises the whole mix.

B1001.heard: A row of beat blocks the second one read. What it is not is a statement spoken and shown on screen of what the film leaves out placed in its first two beats. In this made up example that is by 18 seconds of 82, 22 percent. One level of real play but not a finished game, no save or sound yet, not tested by players. For example, a student's film of their tower defense game says early on that only one map exists.

B1002.heard: A call to action is the last request to the viewer, one concrete thing to try, with a way to check it worked. Here widen the first gap from 3 meters to 4, run the jump test and watch whether Walker still clears it. The check is that the test exits with zero, not a vague try it yourself. For example, a student ends by asking viewers to raise the enemy's speed value and see whether the patrol test still passes.

B1003.heard: Claim versus evidence separates with the film asserts from the capture or output on screen that backs it. The five claims three are backed by clips, the gap, the spike reset and the flag. The claim it runs at 60 frames per second has no measurement on screen and the claim players love it has no play-dest so those two are cut or proved. For example, a student who says their enemy chases the player around a wall shows the captured run of it.

B1101.heard: Each pair sets two look-alike terms side by side. Real-time capture records the game as it runs, so frame times wobble like the uneven dark bars. Render computes each frame offline so every red bar is built to order an even.

B1102.heard: Resolution counts the pixels in one frame, here 40 cells in one picture. Frame rate counts the frames in one second, here 24 pictures. A sharper picture and a smoother motion are different numbers.

B1103.heard: A cut jumps straight to the next shot, so two 5 second clips make 10 seconds. A transition overlaps the two shots, so a 1 second to solve leaves 9.

B1104.heard: A storyboard is pictures in order with no words and no seconds. A beat sheet is pictures, words and seconds, here's 6, 12 and 18 seconds for the first three beats.

B1201.heard: A vague request sits above the exact instruction that replaces it. Make the camera smoother becomes linear keys at 1.25 meters a second and ease only at rest. A sign ease would peak at 1.96 over the limit of 1.5.

B1202.heard: Make it sharper becomes capture natively at 3,840 by 2,160, four times the pixels of 1080p, not 720p scaled up. That is 8.29 million pixels against 2.07 million.

B1203.heard: The voice runs past the shot becomes cut 17 words to 16, so the speech now 6.7 seconds fits the 7 second beat. Speech must end by the time the beat does.

B1204.heard: Keep text away from the edge becomes. Keep text inside the 5% safe area, 192 pixels at the sides, and 108 at top and bottom.

B1205.heard: Make the sound right becomes integrated loudness between minus 28 and minus 18 Luffs and a True Peak below minus 1. One course film measured minus 24.55 with a True Peak of minus 2.96. One window, one ceiling.

B1301.heard: This is a checklist of six questions to ask before you show a walkthrough film. First, does every shot serve the one sentence central idea, a shot that does not is cut.

B1302.heard: Second, does the film say what it is not in its first two beats, spoken aloud and shown on screen as well?

B1303.heard: Third was the route measured before anything was captured. The route check report speed, turn rate and height on every frame against its limits.

B1304.heard: Fourth is every clip real capture of the game. Anything else, such as a mock-up or a staged view, is labeled constructed on screen.

B1305.heard: Fifth, do the words fit each beat and does the sound fit its loudness window. Cut words to fit the beat and measure the film against the window.

B1306.heard: 6. Does every claim in the narration have evidence on screen? Then say it exactly. Not make it smoother, but 1.25 meters a second, linear under 1.5.

BVDT.heard: Let's recap a beat sheet list every beats picture, words and seconds in order. A shot is one take and the route is the whole path. A route check measures speed, turn rate, roll and height on every frame. A fixed frame rate gives every frame the same slice of game time. Resolution is pixels in one frame and frame rate is frames per second. Every claim in the narration needs evidence on screen.

BHTF.heard: Quizme on walkthrough film terms with short cases from filming a game I built one at a time. Use beat sheet, storyboard, shot, route, waypoint, real time capture, render, fixed frame rate, resolution and b-roll. For each case I must name the exact term and say why its look alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply, then tell me if I was right.

BOUT.heard: Key terms the walkthrough film at Nick Bear Brown.
